subject: physics
question_text: Derive an expression for the work done in an isothermal process.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 (Thermodynamics) Short Answer Question 6 (printed p.128). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: for n moles at constant temperature T, W = ∫P dV with P = nRT/V gives W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 2.303 nRT log₁₀(V₂/V₁), positive for an expansion (V₂ > V₁); since the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, ΔU = 0 for an isothermal change, so by the first law ΔQ = W — all the heat supplied becomes work.

steps.label: Setting up the work integral
lines: For n moles of an ideal gas at
from V₁ to V₂, the work done is

lines.text: W = ∫ P dV, V₁ to V₂

lines: with P = nRT/V from the ideal gas
steps.margin_note: Write P in terms of V using PV = nRT before integrating — that is the substitution this step earns.
steps.why: The work integral needs P as a function of V alone; the ideal gas equation at fixed T and n is what supplies that function.
common_mistakes: Leaving P as a constant while integrating — P changes with V during an isothermal expansion, since T is fixed but V is not.
Forgetting the ideal gas equation and trying to integrate P dV with no substitution at all.
steps.memory_tip: Substitute P = nRT/V first — an isothermal integral always starts here.

steps.label: Integrating
steps.margin_note: This is the standard integral ∫dV/V = ln V — the substitution and the antiderivative are this mark; the limits are evaluated in the next step.
steps.why: ∫dV/V is one of the few integrals a student is expected to know outright — recognising it as ln V is the substance of this mark.
common_mistakes: Dropping the constant nRT outside the integral partway through.
Confusing ∫dV/V with ∫V dV — the antiderivative of 1/V is ln V, not V²/2.
steps.memory_tip: ∫dV/V is ln V — know this antiderivative outright.

steps.label: Evaluating between the limits

lines.text: W = nRT[ln V] from V₁ to V₂

lines: For an expansion, V₂ > V₁, so W is
positive: the gas does work ON the
steps.margin_note: The limits substitution gives ln(V₂/V₁); the base-10 form and the sign are part of stating it fully.
steps.why: Evaluating [ln V] between V₁ and V₂ gives ln(V₂/V₁) directly; converting it to 2.303 log₁₀ is the conventional way to present it for numerical work, and stating the sign completes the answer.
common_mistakes: Writing the answer as nRT ln(V₁/V₂), with the limits reversed — that gives the wrong sign for an expansion.
Writing the constant as 2.3 instead of 2.303 — 2.303 is the conventional value.
steps.memory_tip: Upper limit over lower limit, V₂ over V₁ — and 2.303 log₁₀ is the same thing in base ten.

steps.margin_note: State ΔU = 0 BEFORE writing ΔQ = W — the zero is the reason, not an afterthought.
steps.why: This ties the isothermal work formula back to the first law: because internal energy cannot change at constant temperature for an ideal gas, the entire heat input must appear as work.
common_mistakes: Writing ΔQ = W without first establishing ΔU = 0 — the connection is the mark, not just the final equation.
Saying no heat is exchanged in an isothermal process. Heat IS exchanged — all of it turns into work, since none of it raises the internal energy.
steps.memory_tip: Isothermal means ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so every joule of heat leaves again as work.

insider_note: The sign statement — positive for expansion — and the ΔU = 0 reasoning are the two marks students most often skip, even when the formula itself is right.
